General discussion

People use language to signal to others which groups they belong to, partly by speaking like, or aligning with, other members of those groups. But we rarely belong to just one group, and must learn to use language to signal our membership in multiple categories, even when those groups may have conflicting styles of speech. In the current study, we asked whether 7-to 9year-old children's lexical choices (i.e., who they align with) are influenced by the multiple social categories that they belong to, especially when their multiple groups-in this case, their assigned teammates and same-gender peers-used different labels. In line with previous work (St. Pierre et al., 2024), we found that children selectively aligned their language with their assigned in-group (i.e., their teammates), producing labels more like those of their teammates than of their opponents. Specifically, children were more likely to produce labels dispreferred by the broader community (e.g., sofa instead of couch) when their teammates produced dispreferred labels. Given that children heard each label (preferred and dispreferred) the same number of times, and always heard an out-group member immediately before responding, children's preference for in-group labels cannot be explained by automatic, low-level processes (e.g., activation and recency; Pickering & Garrod, 2004), but by a socially selective process tied to children's group affiliation (Wynn et al., 2025).

Most notably, children did not rely on a single group membership when deciding whose language to emulate, but at the same time weighed labels used by both their teammates and same-gender peers. This was seen most clearly in the incongruent condition where team membership and gender membership were pitted against one another (i.e., when children's opposing team had same-gender peers and their own team other-gender peers). In this condition, when teammates did not share the child's gender, their tendency to align with their teammates was attenuated compared to when their teammates matched their gender. Specifically, they adopted their teammates' labels to a lesser extent, and opted instead to sometimes use the contrasting label produced by same gender peers on the opposite team. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that children's lexical alignment is sensitive to the communication patterns of the multiple groups that children belong to.

This particular pattern of results is notable for several reasons. First, rather than categorically aligning with either their teammates or same gender peers on the opposing team, children in the incongruent condition appeared to integrate competing cues in a graded fashion, aligning to some extent with both groups. This is seen both at the group level, where alignment was attenuated by conflicting gender cues rather than reversed (or unchanged from the congruent condition), and also on an individual level, with no evidence of a bimodal distribution of alignment (i.e., children either wholly aligning with one group or the other). This suggests that children do not treat their group memberships as mutually exclusive, but, like adults (e.g., Holliday, 2024; Podesva et al., 2012), can hold and act on more than one membership at the same time through their language use. Although the children in our study made a simple choice between two labels, their behavior may reflect an early capacity to simultaneously index more than one aspect of their identity in their speech.

Second, although children acknowledged both group memberships at once, they nevertheless did weigh one more heavily than the other, specifically team membership over gender, despite previous research suggesting that children prioritize gender over minimal groups (e.g., Yang et al., 2022). Part of this may reflect the fact that gender was never explicitly foregrounded in the experiment. Whereas team membership was overtly established-children were assigned to a colored team of (ostensibly) like-minded peers, and the task was framed as a competition between these different colored teams-gender was conveyed only incidentally through each player's avatar and recorded voice. This experimental emphasis on team membership (rather than gender membership) may have prompted children to generally align more with their teammates than same-gender peers. Work with adults has shown that speakers are more likely to speak in ways that are characteristic of a particular part of their identity if they are in a context that primes or foregrounds that part of their identity (e.g., Hay et al., 2010; see Levon & Katsiveli, 2023). For example, in one study, biracial adults were perceived as sounding more Black when previously primed to talk about their Black parent and more White when previously primed to talk about their White parent (Gaither et al., 2015). Given that gender was never explicitly foregrounded in the experiment, it is in some ways striking that children's word choices were influenced by gender at all. Future work manipulating the extent to which particular social categories are emphasized (e.g., making gender overt and team membership incidental) could help to establish the extent to which children's group-based alignment flexibly varies depending on how social categories are framed in particular contexts (see Wang et al., 2021).

Finally, despite children's lexical choices being influenced by group membership, we should note that overall, children still tended to favor using the preferred term, even in the condition where their gender-matched teammates produced dispreferred terms. In other words, children did not fully align with the dispreferred labels of their teammates, but continued producing preferred labels much of the time. This is consistent with prior work showing that children produce preferred terms to a considerable degree even after exposure to dispreferred labels (Branigan et al., 2016; Hopkins & Branigan, 2020; Hopkins et al., 2017; St. Pierre et al., 2024). Whereas previous work might explain this as a matter of activation, where the priming of dispreferred terms does not always overcome the higher baseline activation of preferred terms, leading to occasional productions of preferred terms, we find it unlikely that the overall preference for preferred labels in our data is completely reducible to low level processes. Instead, given that children heard both labels and were prompted to think about and produce their own response, we think that children continued to sometimes produce preferred terms by choice; however, the reasons why remain unclear. One possibility is that children sometimes preferred the label that they would normally use, despite their teammates using another label, raising questions about how children balance the pressure or desire to conform to their group members while still "being themselves." Another possibility is that children recognized that some labels are more frequent and conventional in the broader community than others, and were sometimes reluctant to follow teammates when they deviated from community norms (Rutland et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2012), raising the possibility that children were responding not only to their team and gender, but to a third group (i.e., the broader speech community whose conventions the preferred term reflects). Future work should examine the extent to which children perceive dispreferred variants to be unconventional and 'marked' (Clark, 1990), and how that influences how they interpret individuals who produce these forms (see Diesendruck et al., 2010).

In sum, the current study shows that by middle childhood, children already track more than one of their group memberships at once and weigh them against each other in deciding whose speech to align with. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that children's lexical alignment is shaped by the language choices of group members from different social categories. How this capacity emerges and scales up in more real-world contexts remains an open and important question at the intersection of developmental and sociolinguistic research.
